Neolithic settlement. This refers to the transition from temporary, mobile camps to permanent villages and towns during the Neolithic period roughly ten thousand to five thousand years ago. This shift was intimately linked to agriculture. Once humans committed to cultivating specific plots of land, they needed year-round residence. Neolithic settlements reveal through archaeology the social innovations—property, cooperation, hierarchy—that permanent habitation required, making them windows into civilization's emergence.

Permanent settlement required abandoning the seasonal mobility of hunter-gatherers. Farmers could not follow herds and had to remain near cultivated fields through growing and harvest seasons. Residential architecture changed fundamentally. Structures became more substantial, featuring stored goods, storage facilities, and defended boundaries. Remains reveal evolution from simple huts to organized housing compounds.

Population concentration at settlements supported specialization. Not all residents farmed. Some made tools, processed food, or performed administrative or religious functions. This marked the beginning of occupational diversity. Property concepts emerged alongside settlement. Farmers invested labor in cleared fields and irrigation systems, creating incentive to defend and inherit land. Settlement archaeology reveals storage structures protecting accumulated grain and tools.

Defensive architecture—walls and fortifications appearing at sites like Jericho—suggests conflict emerged as populations concentrated around resources and stored wealth. Defense became necessary. Social organization became more complex. Permanent settlements required mechanisms to coordinate group labor, manage shared resources, settle disputes, and organize defense. These formed the foundations of political authority.

Gender roles may have shifted with settlement. In mobile forager societies, division of labor was flexible. Sedentary farming societies show archaeological evidence of more specialized and rigid gender-based task allocation. Settlement size varied dramatically. Some Neolithic villages housed only dozens of people, while others like Çatalhöyük accommodated over one thousand residents in densely packed adobe houses, creating diverse patterns of community organization.

Neolithic settlement connects closely to early agriculture, the subsistence base enabling and requiring permanent settlement, and to the broader Neolithic revolution, the cultural transformation of which settlement was a component.
